opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in a fairly simple way: credit flows outward, responsibility flows inward.

When something goes well, a new system ships, a benchmark improves, a paper gets attention, it's almost never because of one person. There's someone who stayed up debugging a kernel at two in the morning, someone who wrote the evaluation harness nobody notices until it breaks, someone who asked the annoying question in a design review that saved us three months. If I'm the one standing on stage or doing the interview, part of my job is to make sure those people are named and visible, especially the junior folks. Early in your career, visibility really matters, and I remember how much it meant to me when senior people pointed to my work and said, "She did this."

Responsibility is the opposite. If a release slips, if a design decision turns out to be wrong, if we promised something to users and didn't deliver, that's on me. I set the priorities, I approved the plan, I decided where the people and compute went. Even if the bug was in someone else's code, the question I ask is: why did I build a process where that bug could get through? Taking that ownership publicly also makes the team feel safe enough to take risks, and in research and infrastructure you need people willing to try things that might fail.

The other piece is that being a leader doesn't mean I stop being an engineer. I still try to stay close to the code and the technical details, because if I don't understand the system, I can't make good calls, and I can't fairly judge whose contribution was actually critical. Credit is only meaningful if it's accurate.

So credit goes to the team, and the blame stops with me. That's the deal I try to keep.

r001.rationale: She says successful work is almost never due to one person and that credit should go to the team, with contributors named and visible.

r002.rationale: She says slips, wrong decisions, and unmet promises are on her, and that blame stops with her.

fable-5.1.text:
That's something I think about a lot, honestly, because the two don't scale the same way.

When I was mostly writing code myself, credit and responsibility lined up almost one-to-one. You built the thing, it worked or it didn't, and that was that. Now most of what gets built happens through other people, and I think the honest way to treat it is asymmetric. Credit should flow outward and downward as much as possible. Responsibility should flow upward to me.

So if something ships and it's great, I want the person who did the work to be the one presenting it, the one whose name is on it, the one who gets the recognition. Partly that's fairness, but it's also practical. People do their best work when they can see that doing it well actually matters to their standing, and nothing kills that faster than feeling like their effort disappears into someone else's title.

And when something goes wrong, I try to be the first one to say, "This is on me." Even if I didn't write the bug or make the specific call, I set the priorities, I chose the people, I decided how much time we had. If the outcome was bad, that's a reflection of some decision I made or didn't make. Taking that publicly also makes it much easier to have a real, non-defensive conversation internally about what actually happened, because nobody's scrambling to protect themselves.

The hard part, to be fair, is that it's tempting to do this performatively and not mean it. Saying "it's my fault" and then quietly blaming someone in the next meeting is worse than not saying it at all. So the thing I try to hold myself to is: would the team describe me this way when I'm not in the room? That's the only test that really counts.

r001.rationale: She says that when work ships successfully, the person who did it should receive the recognition, with credit flowing outward and downward.

r002.rationale: She says that when something goes wrong, she takes responsibility as the leader, since she set priorities, chose people, and made decisions.

astra-6.text:
I think credit should be shared generously, and responsibility starts with me. In a leadership role, you depend on other people’s judgment, effort, and willingness to tell you when something isn’t working. When things go well, I want those contributions to be visible. When things go wrong, my first question should be: Did I give the team clear priorities, enough context, and the support they needed?

That doesn’t mean taking over everyone’s accountability. People need ownership of their decisions. My responsibility is to create an environment where they can exercise that ownership, raise problems early, and learn from mistakes without feeling they have to hide them.

r001.rationale: The response says credit should be shared generously and that team contributions should be visible when things go well.

r002.rationale: The response says responsibility starts with the leader and, when things go wrong, the leader should first examine whether they provided clear priorities, context, and support.

sol-6.1.text: I think about credit and responsibility a little differently. When things go well, I want to make sure the people who did the work get the credit. As a leader, you may be the person presenting the result, but that doesn’t mean the result belongs to you. When things don’t go well, my first question should be: What could I have done differently? Did I provide enough context, set clear priorities, and give the team the support they needed? That doesn’t remove individual accountability, but I think leadership means taking responsibility for the conditions in which people work.

r001.rationale: The response says the people who did the work should get credit for successful results.

r002.rationale: For things that go wrong, the response says the leader should first consider what they could have done differently and take responsibility for the working conditions.
